newsitem.title: USA: Amgen releases long-awaited data on leptin.
newsitem.headline: Amgen releases long-awaited data on leptin.

text.p: Amgen Inc. said Monday that preliminary data on a new obesity drug demonstrated the drug was safe and appeared to produce some weight loss.
While the data were encouraging enough for Amgen to proceed with further trials of the drug, leptin, some industry observers were disappointed there was not a clearer showing of effectiveness.

Although the purpose of the Phase I trials was only to confirm the compound was safe, expectations for the drug have run high since 1995, when Amgen paid an unprecedented $20 million for rights to the gene that produces leptin. Many investors and dieters have pinned their hopes on leptin being a breakthrough weight-loss treatment.

The data released Monday were less conclusive. While obese patients taking leptin in the trial lost weight, those receiving the placebo also lost weight, a result Amgen said was probably due to the nutrition and exercise counseling all trial participants received.

Although those patients receiving leptin lost more weight, Amgen said the difference was not always significant. Among 30 obese people in the trial, for instance, those taking leptin lost an average of four to nine pounds after 90 days, while those on the placebo lost an average of about three pounds.

"I thought it was relatively positive data," said Donaldson Lufkin and Jenrette analyst Alex To. "The main purpose of Phase I trials are to demonstrate the feasibility of further development, and these trials achieved that."

But To said the feeling among industry analysts who spoke with Amgen officials in a conference call after the data came out was generally negative. He said some analysts voiced disappointment at the lack of statistical significance between the leptin and the placebo results.

Amgen shares initially rose in after-hours trading but later fell back to around $62.125, off 62.5 cents, near their level at the close of trading on Nasdaq. The stock has fallen steadily in recent weeks from a high for the year of $69.375, often over uncertainty about the leptin trial.

Along with the weight loss issue, the trial raised some questions about how well the drug was tolerated. Since Amgen is a protein that cannot be absorbed through the stomach, it has to be delivered via injection.

Amgen said the injections were well tolerated at some doses levels, but at higher levels produced side effects, the most common being an irritation at the site of the injection. Although the higher doses produced more weight loss, Amgen said those levels were unacceptable because of the resulting irritation, or the need for an injection more than once a day.

Amgen now plans to begin Phase II trials to further evaluate safety and efficacy and fine tune dosing. As part of the process, it said it plans to work on a second generation leptin molecule that is better tolerated at higher doses.

In addition, it said it will also conduct a Phase II trial to examine whether the drug has added benefits for patients with non-insulin dependent diabetes. Animal tests have shown leptin neutralized diabetes at dose levels smaller than what was needed to produce weight loss.
